chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muawiya, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The one who says, 'O Lord, O Allah, O Lord, O Allah,' until his breath is cut off, it will be said to him, 'At your service! What is your need?'

key_terms.لَبَّيْكَ: At your service / I am here for you

ai.seo_question: What is the reward for repeatedly saying 'O Lord, O Allah' until breath is exhausted?
ai.summary: Recorded in *Al-Kafi* by Shaykh al-Kulayni, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) highlights the spiritual potency of dhikr through repetition until breath ceases, a practice reflecting deep presence of heart. The divine response of 'Labbaik' signifies immediate acceptance, emphasizing that sincere, exhaustive invocation invites God's direct attention to the supplicant's needs. This underscores the Shia emphasis on the efficacy of persistent, heartfelt remembrance as a means of drawing near to the Divine.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Muhammad Bin Isa, from Muawiya, from Abu Baseer, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘The one who says, ‘O Lord<sup>azwj</sup>! O Lord<sup>azwj</sup>!’, until his breath is cut off, it would be said to him, ‘At your service! What is your need?’.
en.sarwar: 3. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn ‘Isa from Mu’awiyah from abu Basir from abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) who has said the following: “
Whoever says, ‘O Lord, O Allah, for one full breath, it is said to him, “Your call is heard and well noticed, ask what kind of help do you need?”’
